title: The Lost Tribes of Israel
lead: The tribes of the northern kingdom that Assyria deported after 732 and 722 BC. The Bible says they are in exile "to this day" (2 Kings 17:23); later Jewish and Christian writers wondered where they went and whether they would return, and many peoples have since claimed to descend from them.

sections.b: Kings records two waves: Tiglath-pileser took the people of Galilee and Gilead (2 Kings 15:29; 1 Chronicles 5:26), and after Samaria fell they were settled in Halah, on the Habor River and in the towns of Media (2 Kings 17:6; 2 Kings 18:11). Sargon II claimed 27,290 deportees from Samaria. Assyrian documents from Gozan, Calah and other sites contain Israelite names, showing some of the exiles there. Not everyone was taken: Hezekiah invites northerners still in the land to his Passover, and Josiah collects temple money from Manasseh and Ephraim and includes Israel in his Passover (2 Chronicles 30:1–11; 2 Chronicles 34:6–9; 2 Chronicles 35:18), and Anna the prophet is from the tribe of Asher (Luke 2:36). The prophets promised that Ephraim and Judah would be one again (Ezekiel 37:15–28). Josephus says the ten tribes were still beyond the Euphrates in his day, an immense multitude too large to count (Antiquities 11.133), and 2 Esdras 13:39–47 imagines them in a far land called Arzareth, waiting to return.

sections.b: Many groups have claimed descent from the lost tribes. The Beta Israel of Ethiopia were linked with the tribe of Dan by Eldad ha-Dani's ninth-century tales and by a 1973 ruling of Israel's Sephardi chief rabbi; genetic studies find mostly local Ethiopian ancestry, so their history as a Jewish community is real but descent from Dan is unproven. The Bene Israel of India's Konkan coast tell of shipwrecked ancestors from the north; the Bnei Menashe of northeast India claim Manasseh and were accepted for return to Israel after formal conversion. In 1650 Menasseh ben Israel's Hope of Israel linked Native Americans with the tribes, and Pashtun legends name Israelite ancestors. British Israelism, a nineteenth-century movement, claimed the British and other northern Europeans as Israel's heirs; historians and linguists find no support for it. Most historians think the deportees were gradually absorbed into the peoples of the Assyrian empire, while many northerners stayed in the land or moved south to Judah.
